title: Reset your SSO password
text: If you forgot the password for the single sign-on portal, open the Okta reset page and email yourself a reset link. The link expires after 30 minutes. Resetting the single sign-on password also unlocks the laptop tools that use the same account. Do not send passwords in Slack.

title: Account locked after failed logins
text: Five failed single sign-on attempts lock the account for 15 minutes. Wait for the lockout to expire, or ask IT in the help-access channel to clear it. A lockout is not the same as a forgotten password. If you still know the password, do not start a reset while the lockout timer is running.

title: Connect to the corporate VPN
text: Install the Northwind VPN client from the device portal, then sign in with single sign-on. Choose the home-office gateway when you are working from home. The first connection can take a minute while device posture is checked. Split tunnel is the default so video calls stay off the VPN.

title: Split tunnel and full tunnel VPN
text: Split tunnel sends only internal hostnames through the corporate VPN. Full tunnel sends all traffic through the gateway and is required on untrusted networks such as conference wifi. Switch modes in the VPN client under Connection profile. Full tunnel is slower. Do not use full tunnel from home unless security asks you to.

title: Create and rotate personal API keys
text: Personal API keys live in the developer console under Credentials. Create a key, copy it once, and store it in your local secret file. Rotate a personal API key every 90 days or immediately if it appears in a log or a pull request. Revoke the old key after the new key is deployed. Keys are tied to you and stop working when you leave the team.

title: API key scopes and least privilege
text: Each personal API key has scopes such as read logs, write flags, or admin models. Ask for the smallest scope that unblocks the task. An admin scope on a laptop key is a security incident even if you never call an admin endpoint. Request extra scopes in the access form and include the ticket id in the key name.

title: Store production secrets in Vault
text: Production secrets belong in Vault, not in git, Docker images, or CI logs. Read them at process start with the service account. Rotate database passwords and signing keys through the Vault UI so the audit log records who changed them. Local development uses the sandbox Vault, which holds fake values only.

title: GitHub Actions CI for Python services
text: Every pull request runs GitHub Actions. The workflow installs the package, runs ruff, and runs pytest. CI must pass before merge. Do not skip hooks to land a fix. If the runner cannot find a dependency, pin it in pyproject.toml rather than installing it ad hoc in the workflow unless a system library is required.

title: Speed up CI with dependency caching
text: If your CI job is slow because pip reinstalls dependencies on every build, cache the pip directory with actions cache keyed on a hash of pyproject.toml. Restore the cache before install. A cache miss is normal after you change a dependency. Do not cache virtualenvs across Python versions.

title: Deploy a service to Kubernetes
text: Deploy a service by merging to main. The pipeline builds a container image, pushes it, and rolls out the Kubernetes Deployment in the staging namespace first. Production follows after the staging checks pass. Set requests and limits in the manifest. Do not kubectl apply from a laptop against production.

title: Roll back a bad production release
text: To undo a bad production release, run the rollback action in the deploy workflow and pick the previous image digest. Kubernetes will roll the Deployment back. Then declare an incident if users were affected. Do not push a revert commit as the only fix while the bad image is still serving traffic.

title: Ship behind a feature flag
text: Ship a risky change behind a feature flag so you can turn it off without redeploying. Default the flag to off in production and on in staging. Name flags after the behavior, not the ticket. Remove the flag within two weeks of a full launch so the code does not keep dead branches.

title: Declare an incident and page on-call
text: If users are down or data may be wrong, declare an incident in the status tool. That pages the primary on-call engineer and opens a bridge channel. Say what broke, when it started, and how you know. You do not need a root cause to page someone. Paging is cheap. A quiet outage is not.

title: Write a blameless postmortem
text: A blameless postmortem covers the timeline, the user impact, what detection missed, and the follow-up actions. Describe systems and decisions, not people to blame. Publish it within five business days. Link the incident channel and the rollback or fix that restored service.

title: On-call expectations and handoff
text: Primary on-call acknowledges a page within 10 minutes. Handoff notes go in the on-call channel before the rotation changes and mention open incidents, noisy alerts, and deploys in flight. Secondary on-call is the backup if the primary cannot reach a laptop. Trading a shift is fine when both people agree in the channel.

title: Query application logs
text: Application logs are in the logging UI under the service name. Filter on trace id when you have a request id from a user report. Do not log secrets, passwords, or full API keys. Retention for debug logs is 14 days. Production errors are kept for 90 days.

title: Service metrics and the RED method
text: Dashboards show rate, errors, and duration for each service. Start there during an incident before you read individual logs. A latency increase with a flat error rate often points at a downstream dependency. Copy the dashboard link into the incident channel so the next person sees the same view.

title: Tune a noisy alert
text: If an alert pages more than twice a week without action, tune it or delete it. Raise the threshold, lengthen the window, or route it to a ticket instead of a page. Document the change in the alert review notes. A noisy alert trains people to ignore real pages.

title: Request GPU quota for training
text: Training jobs use the shared GPU pool. Request a GPU quota in the ML platform form: how many GPUs, which type, and for how many hours. Interactive notebooks are capped at one GPU. Batch training can ask for more but must exit when the job finishes. Idle GPU processes are killed after 30 minutes.

title: Register a model version
text: Push trained weights to the model registry with a version tag, the data snapshot id, and the eval metrics. Production inference only loads versions marked approved. Do not point a service at a local checkpoint path. The registry keeps the last ten versions and the current production alias.

title: How document embeddings are built
text: Semantic search encodes each FAQ document with a sentence embedding model. The optional neural model is all-MiniLM-L6-v2, which maps text to a 384 dimensional vector. Vectors are L2 normalized so inner product equals cosine similarity. The offline test suite uses a hashing embedder instead, so it does not download weights.

title: FAISS index for nearest neighbor search
text: Dense retrieval stores normalized document vectors in a FAISS IndexFlatIP. At query time the query is encoded with the same embedder and FAISS returns the highest inner products. Flat inner product is exact, which is appropriate for a small FAQ. A larger corpus would move to an approximate index and must be rebuilt when vectors change.

title: When lexical BM25 beats dense retrieval
text: BM25 is a lexical baseline. It ranks documents by term frequency and inverse document frequency after tokenization. It is strong when the query reuses the words in the answer, which is common for a FAQ. It misses paraphrases that share no tokens, such as passphrase versus password. Keep BM25 in the comparison so dense retrieval has to earn its place.

title: Reciprocal rank fusion for hybrid search
text: Reciprocal rank fusion combines BM25 and dense rankings without normalizing their raw scores. A document at rank r contributes 1 divided by k plus r, with k usually 60. Scores are summed across the two lists and sorted. Fusion helps when the methods disagree. It is not a learned ranker and it cannot recover a document that both lists buried.

title: Offline retrieval metrics
text: Report recall at k, mean reciprocal rank, and normalized discounted cumulative gain. Recall at k is the fraction of relevant documents that appear in the top k. Mean reciprocal rank rewards the first relevant hit. nDCG uses graded relevance and discounts gains lower in the list. On a tiny hand-labeled FAQ, small gaps between methods are noise.

title: Shared notebook servers
text: Shared notebook servers mount the team data volume as read only. Install extra packages in the user environment, not the base image. Shut the notebook down when you stop for the day so the GPU returns to the pool. Do not copy production secrets into notebook cells.

title: How long training data is retained
text: Raw training datasets are retained for 18 months after the last training job that used them, then deleted unless legal asks us to keep a snapshot. Feature tables in the warehouse follow the table owner policy, which is usually 13 months. Retention does not apply to model weights, which follow the registry rules.

title: Personal data in datasets
text: Do not copy personal data into a training set unless the dataset is tagged pii and stored in the restricted bucket. Email, name, and device identifiers are personal data. Hashing an email with MD5 is not anonymization. Ask privacy review before you join a restricted table to a public feature set.

title: Pull request review norms
text: Keep pull requests small enough to review in one sitting. The description should say what changed and how you tested it. Reviewers look for correctness, tests, and unclear names. A review is a request for changes or an approval, not a rubber stamp. Authors merge their own pull request after CI is green and a reviewer has approved.

title: Python linting with ruff
text: Ruff formats Python and checks the rules in pyproject.toml. Run ruff before you push. CI fails if the formatter would change a file or if a lint rule fires. Prefer a small ignore list over disabling a rule on every line. Do not commit a second formatter config.

title: Build and run the service container
text: The Dockerfile installs the package into a slim Python image and starts uvicorn on port 8000. The default embedder inside the image is the offline hashing embedder so the container does not download model weights at start. Set SEMSEARCH_EMBEDDER to minilm only in an image that has the ml extra installed.

title: ML cost budgets and idle GPU shutdown
text: Each team has a monthly GPU budget. Idle processes are shut down after 30 minutes, and a weekend job needs a budget exception. Check the cost dashboard before you launch a large sweep. A failed job still consumes GPU time. Cancel it when the metric you care about has already collapsed.

title: Batch inference jobs
text: Batch inference reads a table, writes predictions, and can take hours. It is the right path for scoring millions of rows. It is the wrong path for a user who is waiting on a button. Use the online inference service for interactive requests. Batch jobs run on spot capacity and may be preempted, so resume from the last written partition.

title: Online inference latency budgets
text: Online inference endpoints have a p95 latency budget of 200 milliseconds, including the network hop inside the cluster. If the model cannot meet that budget, distill it or move the feature to batch inference. Timeouts return a fallback. They should not retry three times and blow the latency budget.

title: Fine-tune a sentence embedding model
text: The optional fine-tuning script builds query and positive document pairs from the labeled FAQ and trains with multiple negatives ranking loss. In-batch negatives are the other positives in the batch. A few dozen pairs are enough to exercise the code and not enough to beat a pretrained MiniLM model. Expect overfitting if you train for many epochs.

title: Multiple negatives ranking loss
text: Multiple negatives ranking loss trains a bi-encoder so the embedding of a query is closer to its positive document than to the other documents in the batch. You do not need explicit negative rows for the basic form. Hard negatives help later. The loss scale is usually around 20. Shuffle the pairs so one query is not repeated back to back.

title: Ask for help in the right channel
text: Use the help-access channel for account and VPN issues, help-ml for GPU, registry, and notebook issues, and the incidents channel only when a page is already open. Search the FAQ before you ask. Paste the error and what you already tried. Do not direct-message an on-call engineer for a how-to question.

title: Request read access to a dataset
text: Warehouse datasets are closed by default. Request read access in the data portal, name the table, and say what question you are answering. Access lasts 90 days. Personal data tables also need a privacy review. Do not share a downloaded extract in a personal drive.

title: Use the staging environment
text: Staging is a smaller copy of production with fake traffic. Deploy there first. It is safe to break staging during the work day and a bad place to test a destructive migration against data you cannot regenerate. Staging secrets are not production secrets. A green staging check is necessary before a production deploy and it is not sufficient on its own.

title: Database migrations during deploy
text: Ship schema migrations as a backward compatible step before the code that depends on them. Expand, then migrate, then contract. Do not rename a column in the same release that drops the old name. Take a backup or a point in time marker before a migration that rewrites a large table. Practice the rollback on staging.
